notes.b: Societies never stand still. Social change is a significant alteration over time in the structures, institutions, relationships, values or behaviour of a society, in other words in the way a society is organised.
points: In exam terms, social change is change in society caused by law reform, technology or major events. The internet and divorce legislation are good examples.
Change can be gradual, such as the slow shift in attitudes to the role of women or to marriage over several decades, or sudden, such as a new law, a war or a pandemic.
Change can be planned, such as a law or a policy, or unplanned. It happens in every society, but the speed differs from one society to another.

Cultural lag is the gap in time between the appearance of a new material invention and the adjustment of norms, values and institutions to it, because people and organisations take time to catch up. The concept was developed by the sociologist William Ogburn.
notes.tip: If asked to explain social change, say it is change in society caused by law reform, technology or major events, and give an example. Do not confuse it with social mobility (movement of people between groups) or with personal change.

notes.b: Many of the biggest changes come from shifts in how people think and live. These social causes feed one another: more education leads to new attitudes, and new attitudes lead to new family patterns.
points: Changing attitudes and values: there is more acceptance of cohabitation, separation, divorce, lone parenthood, same-sex relationships and diversity, less stigma attached to children born outside marriage, and the Church has less influence than before.

Greater equality for women through better education, careers, financial independence and legal equality changes gender roles at home. The marriage bar, the rule forcing women to leave their jobs on marrying, ended in the civil service in 1973.
Urbanisation is the movement of people from rural areas to towns and cities. It weakens close kin ties and extended family contact and brings new lifestyles.
Towns have better services and facilities, but also more pressure, traffic and anti-social behaviour. Rural depopulation means rural areas can lose services and older people can become isolated.
Education: more people reach second and third level, which changes attitudes, expectations and the value placed on qualifications. Wider access also links to social mobility.

Demographic change means changes in the make-up of the population: falling birth rates, smaller families, later marriage and parenthood, longer life expectancy and an ageing population. These alter the structure of households and the demand for services.

Migration, the movement of people into and out of Ireland, brings new cultures, languages and religions. Cultural diffusion, the spread of ideas, fashions and practices between societies through travel, migration and the media, has a similar effect.

Globalisation, the growth of economic and cultural links between countries, means events and ideas in one country affect others. Social movements and pressure groups also campaign for change, for example for equality, and gain support for their aims.
notes.tip: Name each cause as social, economic or technological, and tie it to an effect on family life with an Irish example. One cause with one effect earns marks.

notes.h: Legal and political causes of change
notes.b: Law reform both reflects change in attitudes and drives it, because a new law changes what people may do and what they come to expect of one another.
points: Divorce: the referendum was held in November 1995 and passed narrowly. The Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996 then set up the legal process. Say referendum 1995, Act 1996, not that divorce was available in 1995.
Same-sex marriage was approved by referendum in 2015 and given effect by the Marriage Act 2015.
The Civil Partnership Act 2010 provided civil partnership for same-sex couples. This was the earlier arrangement, because since 2015 same-sex couples can marry.
Other legal changes that alter family life include maternity and paternity leave and equality legislation, which support parents at work and promote equal treatment.
notes.tip: State only what each law does in one line, and do not give section numbers. Give the referendum year and the Act year separately for divorce.

notes.b: How a society earns its living shapes family life, because work decides who is at home, how much money the household has and where people live.
points: Industrialisation moved many workers from farms and rural trades into factories and towns. Service industries have since grown, and work patterns have changed to include flexible hours, job sharing and working from home.
Growth of female employment has produced dual-earner households. These have more income but more need for childcare, and can bring role overload and role conflict, which are effects, not causes.

Unemployment, recession, emigration and returning emigrants change family life by splitting relatives apart and bringing them back. High housing costs delay home ownership, marriage and parenthood, while higher standards of living improve comfort.
State welfare: improved social welfare, such as child benefit and pensions, reduces dependence on the family and eases financial strain.
notes.tip: Women entering paid work is a cause of changing roles and of dual-earner families. Role overload is an effect, so do not mix them up. For welfare, say it reduces financial strain on families.

notes.b: New technology changes daily life faster than norms and institutions can adjust, which is cultural lag in action. Its effects can be positive and negative.
points: Modern communications technology, including mobile phones, the internet and social media, changes how families communicate, how children learn and how people work, and it changes how people spend leisure time. Examples are children skilled in IT, video calls and apps.
Positive effects include access to information and contact with distant relatives. Negative effects include addiction, cyber-bullying and less face-to-face time.
Labour-saving appliances free time and make shared housework easier, which supports more equal roles at home.
Contraception and medical advances affect family size and life expectancy, because families can plan the number of children and people live longer.
Transport shortens distances, so relatives and workers can live further apart and still keep in touch.
notes.tip: Give a positive and a negative effect of technology, and link each to family life, for example video calls keeping distant relatives in contact against less face-to-face time.

notes.h: Effects of social change on society and the family
notes.b: Social change affects the family, institutions and everyday life, and its effects can be both positive and negative.
points: Changing gender roles: more women take part in paid employment, and household tasks are more often shared between partners, giving more equal roles.
Smaller families: many couples have fewer children or have them later in life, and fewer marriages, and later ones, are taking place.
Changing family structures: lone-parent, blended and cohabiting families have become more common, so family structures are more diverse, and the extended family has declined.
An ageing population increases demand for health and care services and for support for older people, and the roles of older people change. More families use childcare.
Changes in values, such as greater acceptance of diversity, change the norms people expect of one another.

Effects can be positive, such as more choice and freedom, or negative, such as stress and strain, role overload, loss of community and social problems. Rapid change can leave some groups behind, for example people whose skills are no longer needed in changing industries.
Change affects institutions: the Church loses influence, the State takes on more services, and schools adapt to diversity.
Social change can cause tension and conflict between groups that hold different values, for example older and younger generations.
notes.tip: Do not present change as always good or always bad. Give one positive and one negative effect, and keep causes and effects apart.

notes.b: Not everyone welcomes change, and several forces can slow it down or stop it.
points: Vested interests are groups who benefit from the existing system, so they may oppose changes that would reduce their advantages.
Tradition and religious belief can resist changes in norms and values that conflict with long-held teachings.
Fear of the unknown and uncertainty about the consequences of change make people reluctant to accept it.
The cost of change, in money, time and disruption, can slow or prevent it, and generations may disagree about it.

notes.b: Ireland has seen rapid change in recent decades, and each example below links a cause to an effect on family life.
points: Divorce: Irish voters approved divorce by referendum in 1995, and the Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996 provided for it. Marriage equality followed, with a referendum in 2015 and the Marriage Act 2015.
Women in employment: the marriage bar in the civil service ended in 1973, and more married women have been in paid work since, which changed roles at home.
Migration: the Celtic Tiger, a period of rapid economic growth in the late 1990s and 2000s, brought increased immigration and with it new languages, cultures and religions.
Emigration in earlier decades and in the 2008 recession years, and return migration, moved relatives apart and then back together, affecting families and communities.
Rural depopulation and urban growth shifted people from the countryside to towns, and the influence of the Church has fallen.
notes.tip: Tie every change to its effect on family life with a specific Irish example, and say whether it is a social, economic or technological cause.

notes.h: How to answer questions on social change
notes.b: Exam questions on social change usually ask for the impact on family life, and marks are given for each cause covered.
points: Structure a discuss answer by cause (social, economic, technological) and then effect, with one Irish example for each point.
Link each cause to a clear effect, for example urbanisation weakening extended family contact, or dual incomes increasing the need for childcare.
notes.tip: The marking schemes award points per cause, so cover all three categories rather than one in depth.

keyTerms.definition: A significant alteration in the structures, institutions, relationships, values or behaviour of a society over time.
The delay between the appearance of a new material invention and the adjustment of norms and institutions to it.
The movement of people from rural areas to towns and cities.
The development of factory production, which moves workers from farms and rural trades into towns.
The spread of ideas, fashions and practices between societies.
The growth of economic and cultural links between countries, so that changes in one country affect others.
The advantage a group gains from the existing system, which may lead it to oppose change.
Change in the size, age structure or birth rate of a population.

questions.prompt: Outline two causes of social change, giving an example of each.
questions.model: Technological change, for example the spread of the internet and smartphones, which changed how people communicate, work and spend leisure time. Urbanisation, for example the movement of people from rural areas to towns and cities, which loosened close kin ties and brought new lifestyles.

questions.prompt: Discuss the causes and effects of social change in Ireland over recent decades.
questions.model: Causes include technological change, such as the spread of the internet and smartphones; economic change, such as industrialisation and the growth of services, which moved workers from rural trades into towns; urbanisation, which weakened close kin ties; demographic change, such as falling birth rates and an ageing population; and legal change, such as the 1995 divorce referendum and the Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996. Cultural diffusion through migration and the media, and globalisation, also introduced new ideas. Effects include changing gender roles, with more women in paid employment and more shared household tasks; smaller families and later childbearing; changing family structures, including lone-parent and blended families; increased demand for health and care services because of an ageing population; and changing values, such as greater acceptance of diversity. Change can cause tension between generations and leave some groups behind when their skills are no longer needed. Resistance from vested interests, tradition and fear of the unknown can slow change, and cultural lag can mean norms take time to catch up with technology.
